prompt.context: Your client is Yoga Jones, the owner of Orange Yoga Studio. Orange Yoga is a very popular, up-scale yoga studio in New York City known for high quality instruction and a relaxed vibe. Yoga Jones has owned and operated Orange Yoga for the past 5 years. For its first four years, Orange Yoga was very financially successful; however in the past year, Yoga Jones noticed that her profits are declining. She doesn't keep very good financial records and has made a few big investments lately, so is having a hard time figuring out a) whether she is actually losing profit and b) how to fix her financial problems.
prompt.question: How do you help Yoga Jones?

clarifying_info.q: What classes does Orange Yoga offer and how often?
clarifying_info.a: Orange Yoga offers 5 classes daily on weekdays and 4 classes on weekends. All classes are Vinyasa Flow style.
Clients pay on a per-class basis. There are currently no package deals or membership rates.
The competitive landscape for yoga studios in NYC has remained unchanged over the past three years.
Major maintenance upgrades: hardwood floors, fresh paint, and new shower facilities. These were financed primarily through loans.

No variable costs on a per-customer basis — all costs are fixed. Five main fixed costs: Rent/utilities = $3,500/month; Liability insurance = $1,800/year; Administration costs (owner salary, supplies, computer system, marketing) = $800/week; Yoga instructor salaries = $50/class; Loan payments = $500/month.

Class fees are the only source of revenue. All classes cost $12. Average of 8 students per class on weekdays and 6 students per class on weekends. Assume every month has 22 weekdays and 8 weekend days.

exhibits.title: Average number of weekday students in Orange Yoga classes
exhibits.shows: Two charts about weekday attendance: (1) a bar chart of average number of weekday students per class time slot in 2014 across five time slots (7am, 10am, 12pm, 6pm, 8pm); (2) a line chart showing trends in average weekday students per class time slot from 2010 to 2014 for those same five time slots.
exhibits.data: Y-axis goes from 0 to 12 students; five time slots shown: 7am, 10am, 12pm, 6pm, 8pm; trend lines span 2010–2014; max average appears to peak near 10 students

exhibits.title: Average number of weekend students in Orange Yoga classes
exhibits.shows: Two charts about weekend attendance: (1) a bar chart of average number of weekend students per class time slot in 2014 across four time slots (10am, 12pm, 6pm, 8pm); (2) a line chart showing trends in average weekend students per class time slot from 2010 to 2014 for those same four time slots.
exhibits.data: Y-axis goes from 0 to 12 students; four time slots shown: 10am, 12pm, 6pm, 8pm; trend lines span 2010–2014; max average appears to peak near 10 students

framework: Revenue: price per class × number of classes × students per class (weekday vs. weekend separately)
Costs: fixed costs only — rent, insurance, admin/owner salary, instructor salaries per class, loan payments
Other considerations: popularity trends, marketing, alternative revenue streams (products, memberships, private classes)

questions.prompt: Calculate monthly revenue for Orange Yoga.
questions.guidance: Candidate should separate weekday and weekend revenue, multiply price × classes per day × students per class × days in month, then sum.

math.setup: Weekday revenue: $12/class × 5 classes/day × 8 students/class × 22 weekdays. Weekend revenue: $12/class × 4 classes/day × 6 students/class × 8 weekend days.

questions.prompt: Calculate monthly costs for Orange Yoga.
questions.guidance: Candidate should convert all costs to a monthly basis, then sum. Five cost categories: rent/utilities, insurance, admin, instructor salaries (weekday + weekend separately), loan payments.

math.setup: Rent: $3,500/month. Insurance: $1,800/12 = $150/month. Admin: $800/week × 4 = $3,200/month. Instructor weekday: $50/class × 5 classes/day × 22 days. Instructor weekend: $50/class × 4 classes/day × 8 days. Loan: $500/month.

questions.prompt: Is Orange Yoga profitable? What is the monthly profit/loss?
questions.guidance: Candidate subtracts costs from revenue to show a monthly loss of ~$1,650. This confirms Yoga Jones is indeed losing money.

questions.prompt: Brainstorm: After analyzing her books, Yoga Jones discovers her decline in profit began after a $2,000/month rent increase last year and a decision to raise all teacher salaries by $10/class. She does not want to move and believes strongly in paying her teachers a high wage. What else can she do?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm revenue-side and cost-side levers. Strong candidates will naturally propose multiple categories before being prompted.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 1 (charts on class-level attendance): What insights can you draw from the weekday and weekend attendance charts?
questions.guidance: Candidate should separate weekday vs. weekend analysis. Key weekday insight: midday classes (10am, 12pm) have lower attendance than morning and evening; 10am classes may not cover instructor salary. Key weekend insight: midday classes are the most popular while evening classes may not cover instructor salary. Strong candidates note the max average peaks at 10 for both weekday and weekend. Should hypothesize restructuring class times, eliminating unprofitable classes, and adding capacity in popular time slots.

questions.prompt: Yoga Jones currently caps classes at 10 students. Her studio is 13 ft long and 21 ft wide. An average yoga mat is 6 ft long and 2 ft wide. Minimum distance between two mats = 1 ft; minimum distance between a mat and a wall = 6 inches. How many mats can she fit?
questions.guidance: Candidate should draw this out spatially. Each mat with minimum clearance requires 7 ft × 3 ft = 21 sq ft of space. Studio area = 13 × 21 = 273 sq ft. 273 ÷ 21 = 13 mats. However, the mathematical approach does not always hold spatially; the true max is 13 but 12 is also acceptable if the candidate acknowledges wasted space. The instructor does not need a mat.

math.setup: Studio: 13 ft × 21 ft = 273 sq ft. Each mat footprint with minimum clearance: (6 + 0.5 + 0.5) ft long × (2 + 0.5 + 0.5) ft wide = 7 ft × 3 ft = 21 sq ft.
steps: Spatial layout verification required; 12 is also acceptable with acknowledged wasted space
math.answer: 13 mats (or 12 if candidate acknowledges spatial constraints)

questions.prompt: Assume all classes currently at 10 students have a lengthy waiting list. If Yoga Jones increases class size to the maximum you calculated, will this be enough to save the studio?
questions.guidance: Candidate compares new revenue from additional students to the current monthly loss of $1,650. Works for both 12-mat and 13-mat answers. Strong candidates should also mention cutting unprofitable classes and adding evening classes.

math.setup: Current loss: ~$1,650/month. Costs remain unchanged. New revenue from additional students in full weekday and weekend classes.
steps: If max = 12: New weekday students = 12 − 8 = 4 additional per class? (Note: the casebook shows 6 new on weekdays and 4 new on weekends assuming only peak classes at capacity gain students — but using the simpler reading: all 5 weekday classes gain 2 students = 2×5×22×$12 = $2,640 — casebook uses: 6 new students weekday × 22 days × $12 = $1,584; 4 new weekend × 8 days × $12 = $384; total = $1,968 — barely profitable)
If max = 13: 9 new weekday × 22 × $12 = $2,376; 6 new weekend × 8 × $12 = $576; total = $2,952 — clearly profitable
Both scenarios exceed the $1,650 monthly loss, so yes, increasing class size is sufficient to turn a profit
math.answer: Yes — with 12-mat cap: +$1,968 new revenue (barely profitable); with 13-mat cap: +$2,952 new revenue (comfortably profitable)

brainstorming.prompt: Yoga Jones cannot raise teacher salaries further and will not move. What else can she do to improve profitability?

categories.name: Revenue — Pricing
ideas: Variable pricing: charge more for peak classes (evening) or premium clients
Introduce package deals or memberships to lock in recurring revenue

categories.name: Revenue — Product Diversification
ideas: Offer higher-priced class formats (pilates, barre, private sessions)
Add teacher-training programs at a premium price
Sell related products: yoga mats, water bottles, apparel

categories.name: Revenue — Volume
ideas: Add more class time slots, especially in high-demand evening windows
Recruit more students through marketing or referral programs

categories.name: Cost — Reduction
ideas: Eliminate unprofitable classes (those where revenue < instructor salary)

categories.name: Cost — Note: Low Impact
ideas: Refinancing loans is not a great idea — loan payments are already small relative to other costs

recommendation: Increase maximum class size from 10 to 12–13 students per class to capture the waiting-list demand in peak evening and morning slots — this alone generates $1,968–$2,952 in additional monthly revenue, turning the studio profitable
Eliminate classes where average attendance does not cover the instructor's $50 salary (specifically 10am weekday classes and evening weekend classes based on Exhibit 1)
risks: Long-term clients who valued the studio's small, intimate class sizes may be dissatisfied and churn
Clients who depended on flexible class times (now eliminated) may leave
Teachers whose classes are eliminated may be upset, risking retention of valued instructors
next_steps: Communicate class size changes to existing clients with emphasis on maintained quality and instructor expertise
Offer a limited early-access sign-up for loyal clients to secure spots in newly expanded classes
Explore additional revenue levers outside this analysis: price increases, membership/package pricing, product sales, private or specialty classes
Monitor attendance and revenue monthly to assess whether further adjustments are needed
